Series::renorm¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::renorm(double p, std::int64_t dim, double maxnorm) const
Series Series::renorm(double p) const
Series& Series::renorm_(double p, std::int64_t dim, double maxnorm) const
Series& Series::renorm_(double p, std::int64_t dim, double maxnorm) const

What It Does¶

Caps the norm of every sub-tensor along one axis.

Pick an axis dim. Each index along that axis selects a sub-tensor — for a [rows, cols] matrix and dim = 0, that is each row. renorm computes the p-norm of every such sub-tensor and, for any whose norm exceeds maxnorm, scales the whole sub-tensor down so its norm lands exactly on maxnorm. Sub-tensors already within the cap are passed through untouched.

The classic use is keeping the rows of an embedding table from growing without bound during training: after each step, weights.renorm_(2, 0, max_norm) pulls any over-long row back onto the ball of radius max_norm and leaves the rest alone.

Three forms:

  • renorm(p, dim, maxnorm) — the full form.

  • renorm(p) — a convenience: dim = 0, maxnorm = 1. Caps each row at unit norm.

  • renorm_(p, dim, maxnorm) — the in-place form. Mutates the receiver and returns a reference to it.

The norm of a sub-tensor is taken over every axis except dim, so for a higher-rank input each dim-slice is flattened before its norm is measured.

Parameters¶

p (double): which norm to constrain — 1, 2, any positive real. Must be > 0.

dim (std::int64_t): the axis whose sub-tensors are normalized. Negative values count from the end.

maxnorm (double): the ceiling. Sub-tensors with norm above this are rescaled to hit it exactly; maxnorm = 0 zeroes every non-zero sub-tensor. Must be >= 0.

Returns¶

Series Same shape and dtype as the input, in float64 precision internally then cast back. renorm_ returns Series& to the mutated receiver.

The input must have at least 2 dimensions.

Gradient¶

Differentiable. For a sub-tensor left untouched the gradient passes straight through. For a rescaled sub-tensor the scale factor maxnorm / norm itself depends on the data, so the backward carries both the direct scale * grad term and the contribution through the shrinking factor.

In-Place Form¶

renorm_() is the in-place sibling of renorm(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — renorm_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 4.0}, {6.0, 8.0}});
x.renorm_(2.0, 0, 1.0);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.59999999, 0.79999998],
  [0.59999999, 0.79999999]]

Examples¶

Example 1. dim = 0: each row is a vector; the over-long ones are pulled in.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 4.0},     // 2-norm 5  -> rescaled
                             {0.3, 0.4},     // 2-norm 0.5 -> kept
                             {6.0, 8.0}});   // 2-norm 10 -> rescaled
std::cout << x.renorm(2.0, 0, 2.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1.2, 1.6],
  [0.3, 0.4],
  [1.2, 1.6]]

Row 0 was scaled by 2/5, row 2 by 2/10, row 1 (already under 2) is verbatim.

Example 2. Confirm the contract: each rescaled row now has norm exactly maxnorm, each kept row is unchanged.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 4.0}, {0.3, 0.4}, {6.0, 8.0}});
auto y = x.renorm(2.0, 0, 2.0);
std::cout << "row 2-norms = " << y.mul(y).sum(1).sqrt();

Output¶

row 2-norms = pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 0.5, 2]

The cap is a ceiling, not a target — row 1 keeps its norm of 0.5.

Example 3. dim = 1 treats each column as the sub-tensor instead.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 0.3},
                             {4.0, 0.4}});   // col 0 norm 5, col 1 norm 0.5
std::cout << x.renorm(2.0, 1, 2.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[1.2, 0.3],
  [1.6, 0.4]]

Column 0 (norm 5) is scaled by 2/5; column 1 (norm 0.5) is left alone. Same data as Example 1 transposed, and the result is the transpose too.

Example 4. p = 1 caps the sum of absolute values of each row.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{1.0, -2.0, 3.0},   // L1 = 6 -> scaled by 4/6
                             {0.5,  0.5, 0.0}});  // L1 = 1 -> kept
std::cout << x.renorm(1.0, 0, 4.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.66666666, -1.3333333, 2],
  [0.5, 0.5, 0]]

p only changes which norm is measured and constrained; the rescale is still a single scalar multiply per row, so signs and ratios within a row are preserved.

Example 5. The one-argument form: p only, with dim = 0 and maxnorm = 1.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 4.0}, {0.6, 0.8}});
std::cout << x.renorm(2.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.59999999, 0.79999998],
  [0.6, 0.8]]

Row 0 (norm 5) becomes a unit vector; row 1 already has norm 1, so renorm leaves it exactly as it was — the cap is >, not >=.

Example 6. Gradient flows through the scaling.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 4.0}, {6.0, 8.0}});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.renorm(2.0, 0, 2.0).sum().reverse();
std::cout << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.064000005, -0.04799999],
  [0.032000001, -0.023999998]]

The sensitivities are small and mixed in sign because rescaling a row does two things at once: it shrinks the row (a positive push along the direction that grows the sum) and it makes the shrink factor maxnorm / norm respond to the row’s own components (a negative pull back). Both rows started over the cap, so both receive a gradient.

Example 7. A 1-D input is rejected — renorm needs an axis to hold the sub-tensors and an axis to take the norm over.

try {
  auto y = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}).renorm(2.0, 0, 1.0);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

renorm: expected input with at least 2 dimensions

Example 8. maxnorm = 0 zeroes every non-zero sub-tensor.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 4.0}, {0.0, 0.0}});
std::cout << x.renorm(2.0, 0, 0.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 0],
  [0, 0]]

Row 0 has norm 5 > 0 so it is scaled to zero; row 1 already has norm 0, so it is “within” the cap and untouched (still zero).

Example 9. The in-place form mutates the receiver and returns it.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 4.0}, {6.0, 8.0}});
x.renorm_(2.0, 0, 2.0);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[1.2, 1.6],
  [1.2, 1.6]]

Both rows were over the cap, so both are pulled onto norm 2.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The norm of a sub-tensor is taken over every axis except dim. dim is the axis you are indexing into to pick a sub-tensor, not the axis you reduce. renorm(2, 0, m) normalizes rows; renorm(2, 1, m) normalizes columns.

  • The cap is strict-greater: a sub-tensor whose norm equals maxnorm exactly is left alone, not rescaled.

  • Input must be at least 2-D. To cap a single vector’s norm use clamp_max on its norm, or x.unsqueeze(0).renorm(...).

  • maxnorm = 0 collapses every non-zero sub-tensor to zeros.

  • The computation runs in float64 and casts back, so a low-precision input round-trips through float64 (visible as trailing ...9999 in the examples).

  • renorm_ mutates in place — do not call it on a tensor that other live tensors view.

Summary¶

renorm(p, dim, maxnorm) caps the p-norm of every sub-tensor along dim:

  • each dim-slice with norm > maxnorm is scaled down to hit maxnorm exactly; the rest pass through

  • the norm is measured over all axes except dim

  • renorm(p) is the shorthand for dim = 0, maxnorm = 1

  • renorm_ is the in-place form

  • input must be 2-D or higher; differentiable

See Also¶

  • Series::norm: the norm renorm measures and constrains.

  • Series::dist: the other norm-constraint neighbor — the p-norm distance between two tensors.

  • Series::clamp_max: cap raw values; renorm caps a norm.

  • Series::standardize: a different per-row rescale — to unit variance rather than to a norm ceiling.
